findings.title: Sourcemaps with full `sourcesContent` are emitted into the dist that the host serves
findings.detail: `sourcemap: true` writes `.js.map` files beside every chunk in `apps/web/dist`, and `frontend-static` deliberately MIME-maps `.map` to `application/json`, so they are served over the same `/` origin as the app. `package.json`'s `files: ["dist", "!dist/**/*.map"]` and `.npmignore`'s `*.map` only strip the maps from the **npm tarball** — they do nothing for the served directory, and `apps/cli`'s `cf web` serves `apps/web/dist` directly. Verified on the built tree: `dist/assets/index-BKSebiLg.js.map` (1.0 MB) carries `sourcesContent` for `packages/client/web/lib/index.js`, `packages/client/ui-primitives/lib/index.js`, `packages/client/ui-slots/lib/index.js` and `apps/web/src/main.ts`. The host-side request fence keeps this off the network for anonymous callers, but any script executing at the loopback origin (an XSS, a malicious plugin bundle from the client-module system, which is loaded as same-origin script) gets the full original sources with no extra request. Gate the maps behind a build profile the way `CF_BUILD_CLIENT_PROFILE` already gates the official environment.

findings.title: Static responses carry no Cache-Control, ETag or Last-Modified, so content-hashed assets are never cache-validated
findings.detail: The same `writeHead(200, { 'content-type': type })` sets no freshness or validator headers. Vite emits content-hashed filenames (`vendor-CGZwCgY8.js`, 745 KB; `index-BKSebiLg.js`, 390 KB) precisely so they can be marked immutable, but nothing marks them, and there is no ETag/Last-Modified path back to a cheap 304. Meanwhile `index.html` — the one mutable document that names which hashed assets exist — gets no `no-cache`, so a client that does cache it heuristically can reference assets a rebuild has already rotated away, producing a blank shell until a hard reload. Splitting on the `/` root and the configured index from ordinary assets fixes both sides in one place.

findings.title: The `script`/`style`/`html` injection-row kinds splice caller text verbatim while their type contract only documents the invariant
findings.detail: `renderRow` escapes `<` to `<` for the `global` kind specifically so a row-controlled string cannot break out of its script element — the correct treatment, applied to exactly one of the four kinds. `script`, `style` and `html` interpolate `row.text` / `row.html` directly into `<script>`, `<style>` and the document, while their JSDoc merely states "text must not contain `</script`" with no runtime check. Today's only producers are safe (`bootInjections` builds a static template plus a JSON-stringified constant; `bootThemeInjection` interpolates a schema-validated enum), so this is not currently exploitable — but this is the one injection boundary in the whole web app, the contract is unenforced, and any future plugin that pushes a row containing model- or user-derived text gets a document breakout with no failure at the boundary. One `assert` in `renderRow` closes it permanently.

findings.title: WebSocket downlinks register no heartbeat, so a silently dropped client leaves its event-stream subscription open indefinitely
findings.detail: `upgrade()` wires exactly three one-shot listeners — `close`, `error`, and a `message` guard that rejects client traffic with 1008. There is no ping/pong interval and no idle deadline anywhere on the class, and `this.server.clients` is only drained by an explicit `terminate()` inside `close()`, which runs at plugin disposal. A client whose TCP path breaks without a FIN (laptop sleep, Wi-Fi roam, a suspended VM) leaves the socket in `this.server.clients` and, more importantly, leaves the `api.events.mux()` / `api.events.host()` async iterator that `pump` is iterating subscribed on the host. On a long-lived local daemon that is an unbounded accumulation of live stream subscriptions and their buffers. `ws` exposes `ping()`/`pong` on the server side; a 30s interval that terminates a socket with no pong in the window is the standard fix and needs no protocol change.

findings.title: `clientBuildEnvironment` inlines every `CF_CLIENT_*` env var into the browser bundle with no allowlist
findings.detail: `clientBuildEnvironmentDefines`, consumed by `apps/web/vite.config.ts`, turns every environment variable whose name starts with `CF_CLIENT_` into a literal `define` substitution in the shipped JavaScript. The only thing standing between an environment variable and the public bundle is the name prefix — `CF_CLIENT_API_KEY`, `CF_CLIENT_TOKEN` or `CF_CLIENT_SECRET` would all be inlined verbatim by a plain `npm run build:web` or `npm run cf web`. The exact-key-set assertion (`assertClientBuildEnvironment`) exists but is only exercised by the `official` CI profile; a developer-machine or ad-hoc build runs the unfiltered path with no check at all. Replace the prefix filter with an explicit allowlist (`CF_CLIENT_TITLE`, `CF_CLIENT_COMMIT_HASH`, `CF_CLIENT_BUILD_PROFILE` — the three the official profile actually names) and fail the build on any other `CF_CLIENT_*` variable rather than silently publishing it.

findings.title: The browser-trust fence has no end-to-end coverage over a live HTTP server
findings.detail: `isTrustedApiRequest` is the DNS-rebinding and cross-site defense for the entire `/api` surface, and its only coverage is `packages/client/connection/tests/api-request-trust.host.spec.ts` — 108 lines of assertions against the pure predicate with hand-built header objects. The next layer up, `node-half.host.spec.ts:22-29`, stubs `register`/`registerUpgrade` entirely, so the wiring in `connection/src/index.ts` (the route handler's `isTrustedApiRequest(req, trustedHosts)`, the privileged-method re-check with an empty trust list, the upgrade rejection path) is never observed over real HTTP. And the one web-lane test that *does* boot the real `cf web` server only asserts the happy path — that the ready line is a loopback URL and that `fetch` returns 200. Nothing in the repo ever sends a rebound Host, a cross-site `Origin`, or a `sec-fetch-site: cross-site` marker at the live server and asserts 403. A regression that drops the fence would go green everywhere.

findings.title: `clientDocumentTitle` silently no-ops if the title placeholder ever drifts
findings.detail: The plugin rewrites the document title by string-replacing the literal `<title>CF Local Build</title>`. If that exact substring is absent — someone edits `index.html`'s title, or a Vite/react plugin reorders `transformIndexHtml` ahead of this one and normalizes the element — `String.replace` matches nothing and the build succeeds with the placeholder title in the shipped artifact. Official builds set `CF_CLIENT_TITLE=CodeFusion` and assert that environment through `assertClientBuildEnvironment`, so the environment is checked while the HTML substitution it exists to perform is not. `smoke-real.e2e.ts` only asserts `document.title` *after* the running app has rewritten it, and no test pins the built `dist/index.html`'s title. Throw (or at least warn) when the placeholder is missing.

findings.title: The HTTP bridge collapses multi-valued response headers when re-emitting them onto the node response
findings.detail: `Object.fromEntries(response.headers.entries())` produces one value per header name, so any header the upstream `Response` carries more than one of is silently reduced to its last value. Today the `/api` responses only set single-valued headers (`content-type`, `cache-control`, and the 426 upgrade pair), so nothing is broken yet — but `session.export` already returns a Response assembled from the attachment/download path, and `set-cookie`-style multi-value headers cannot survive this bridge if a future route needs them. Node's `res.setHeader(name, string[])` accepts arrays; passing the raw header list through rather than a folded map removes the foot-gun at no cost.

clusters.summary: These secondary packages are, on the whole, unusually well-engineered: fail-loud config validation, cross-realm clone guards at the VM boundary, turn-enclosed audit pairs for approvals and hooks, compare-and-set goal/task revisions, and content-addressed attachment storage with real durability barriers. The weaknesses cluster in the lifecycle edges rather than the happy paths. The most serious theme is missing cancellation/settlement coordination around asynchronous activations and hook-driven control flow: a blocking Stop hook can drive the agent loop forever (both bridges hardcode stop_hook_active to false and have no continuation cap), and cordis_undefine/cordis_stop will happily delete a plugin out from under an in-flight host-half activation, permanently orphaning a live fiber with registered tools and handlers that nothing can ever dispose. The second theme is hot-path cost: both hook bridges copy and scan the entire session event log on every single tool call even when no hook matched, and the experimental agent-team journal re-runs a zod-validated full-log fold on every mailbox/task/roster read. The third is that the Cordis dynamic-package sandbox is honestly labelled non-containment, but the specific invariants the guard facade claims to enforce (no Context escape, nothing invocable) are bypassable by construction through any host-realm function, leaving the once-per-plugin human approval of the client half as the only real gate, and that grant covers all future package versions. I found no path-traversal, zip-slip, or base64/serialization bugs in the attachment, workspace, or skill-filesystem surfaces, and no permission-decision inversion in the hook merge logic.

findings.title: Blocking Stop hook force-continues the turn forever with no cap and a hardcoded stop_hook_active of false
findings.detail: Both bridges map a deny decision at the agent/turn-stopping extension point to agent.steer(), which enqueues into inbox.nextStep. In core/agent-loop/src/agent.ts the step loop only breaks when turnEnds is set and inbox.nextStep is empty, so the steer creates another step, which ends, which re-fires agent/turn-stopping, which runs the Stop hook again. There is no consecutive-continuation counter, no backoff, and no run-level halt; the code's own TODO admits it. Worse, stop_payload always sends stop_hook_active as false, so the standard Claude Code loop-guard idiom (a Stop hook that exits 2 only when stop_hook_active is false) can never detect that it is already inside a forced continuation. A single misconfigured exit-2 Stop hook therefore spins the agent in an unbounded model-call loop until the user cancels, burning tokens and never letting the session end. The Codex twin has the identical defect at hooks-codex/src/index.ts lines 260-270 with its own TODO.

findings.title: undefine and stop do not cancel or await an in-flight host-half activation, orphaning a live fiber with registered tools
findings.detail: activate() at line 810 registers its promise in this.starting and then awaits startFresh(), which itself awaits evaluateHostCode and startHostHalf (group.await plus fiber.await) before assigning plugin.run. Neither undefine (line 210) nor stop (line 456) touches this.starting: undefine computes wasRunning from plugin.run which is still undefined mid-start, retract() no-ops, and registry.delete removes the only handle to the plugin. The in-flight startFresh then completes and sets plugin.run on the now-unregistered object, emits cordis/dynamic-package, and leaves a live fiber hanging under the shared cordis-dynamic group with its harness.handle methods and any registered tools still live. Because the plugin is gone from the registry, no later stop, undefine, or inspect can ever find or dispose it, so the removal guarantee advertised in the cordis_undefine tool description is silently violated. stop is worse UX-wise: it returns not-running for a plugin that starts a moment later.

findings.title: Runs left in starting-host or client-pending are never reconciled, permanently wedging the plugin in transition-in-flight
findings.detail: reconcileApprovals only surfaces a Host run whose latest attempt is awaiting-approval, starting-host, or client-pending AND whose package row is still resolvable. A run parked in starting-host or client-pending has no page-side plan and no approval answer, so nothing ever calls resolveRequestRun for it; the request stays armed in the Host registry forever. Any subsequent cordis_run for that plugin is then rejected by resolvePlan starting check and by run pendingRequestFor with transition-in-flight, so the plugin can never be started again in that process. The realistic trigger is a browser tab closing mid-activation (after runHostHalf returns starting-host but before the page settles the client half) or a page that throws between the two. There is no timeout, no page-liveness probe, and no host-side reaper for these orphans.

findings.title: The sandbox ctx and tool facade is escapable through any host-realm function, so the guard stated invariants are unenforceable
findings.detail: guardedService at line 685 and the ctx facade at line 753 wrap host objects in host-realm Proxies and forward host functions wrapped in host-realm arrow functions. From inside the VM sandbox, any of those values yields the host realm: calling .constructor.constructor on ctx.on, or on ctx.tools, returns the host Function and gives full process access with no require trap needed. The tool-registry facade docblock claims the purpose is that package code cannot call another tool directly and bypass ToolRuntime.execute (identity protection, pre-policy, monotonic guards, around dispatch, post-policy, final observation) and that get returns nothing invocable; that invariant does not hold against a non-cooperative package. The module header does admit host-realm helper functions remain an escape route, but the practical consequence is that the only real control is the human approval gate in the host runner, and that gate is granted once per plugin and then clientVersionUpdatesApproved silently extends it to every future package version of that plugin (index.ts lines 348-351), so a user who approved a harmless v1 UI card is authorizing arbitrary host-side code in v2 without ever being asked again.

findings.title: lastTurn copies and scans the entire session event log on every tool call, before any hook is known to match
findings.detail: lastTurn does an array spread of agent.session.events plus findLast over every session event, including every tool-result blob and message body. Both bridges call it eagerly at the top of the tools/pre-execute and tools/post-execute listeners, so it runs once per tool call per bridge regardless of whether any PreToolUse or PostToolUse group is configured or will match. On a long session with tens of thousands of events and hundreds of tool calls this is a measurable per-call tax on the guard path, duplicated across both dialects. The Codex bridge additionally calls turnBase (which calls lastTurn again) while the surrounding closure already has turn in scope. Compounding it, runPoint awaits each matching hook strictly serially inside the nested group and hook loops with a 10-minute default per-hook timeout, so N matching hooks can hold a single tool call for up to N times 10 minutes with no per-point wall-clock budget.

findings.title: evaluateHostCode misclassifies any runtime-thrown sandbox SyntaxError as a parse failure and returns misleading bracket-balance advice
findings.detail: runInContext of an async IIFE returns a promise, so a SyntaxError thrown inside the package's own running code (a direct throw new SyntaxError, a JSON.parse or new Function the package invokes at runtime, or any host-realm intrinsic that rejects with one) rejects the awaited promise and is then caught by the same handler as a compile failure. isSyntaxError is name-based across realms precisely so sandbox-realm compile errors are detected, but it cannot distinguish compile-time from runtime. The result is rethrown as a failed-to-parse error with the TypeScript-removal and bracket-balance hint from parseErrorMessage, which points the model at the wrong fix entirely and hides the real runtime failure. The existing test at tests/sandbox.spec.ts line 211 only asserts the message format for a runtime SyntaxError, not that the classification is wrong.

findings.title: TeamJournal.state re-validates and re-folds the entire Lead session log on every read
findings.detail: state() calls foldTeam over the whole Lead session log, which walks every event in that log, not just the four team event types, and runs a zod parse on each team-owned event. There is no incremental cache or observedSeq, in contrast to GoalService.sync in packages/goal/goal/src/index.ts lines 437-447 which does exactly this correctly. The cost is paid on every mailbox.send transaction, every markDelivered, every taskBoard get list update and create, every roster.list, and worst of all messagePrecedes in mailbox.ts lines 274-277, which additionally allocates the full message-id array and runs indexOf twice, so the ordering check for a quiet delivery is itself O(events plus messages). A team session that has run for a while therefore degrades quadratically with log length on the hot message path.

findings.title: orchestrate publishes inFlight only after its first await, so a re-entrant open starts a second unguarded activation
findings.detail: orchestrate sets this.activity, then calls this.drive(plan) which begins executing synchronously up to its first await, and only afterwards assigns this.inFlight. The serialization check at the top, which returns early when inFlight already has an entry for the plugin, therefore cannot see an activation that has already begun. Any re-entrant call for the same plugin arriving before that microtask, such as a second open from a duplicate cordis/request-run event, or reconcileApprovals running off a subscription that fires during the same turn, passes the guard, overwrites the activity entry, and launches a second drive that races the first on runHostHalf, getClientCode and load. The host-side resolvePlan and pendingRequestFor checks are the only remaining backstop, and they do not cover the direct-panel path where requestId is undefined.

findings.title: A deadline that fires after the tool has already resolved converts a successful result into a spurious TOOL_TIMEOUT
findings.detail: The wrapper arms deadline and, after awaiting next, unconditionally replaces whatever came back with toolTimeoutResult whenever timeoutOf reports the scoped code. There is no check that the result was actually an abort-shaped result. If a tool completes successfully just before the timeout but the timer callback runs before the awaiting continuation is resumed, the model is told the call timed out even though the work completed and its side effects are committed. For a non-idempotent tool such as a write, a shell command, or an API charge, the model natural recovery is to retry, producing a duplicate side effect. The comment above the check already assumes the tool saw the abort and reached quiescence; that assumption is not verified anywhere in the wrapper.

findings.title: subagentChildren retains strong Agent references released only by a subagent/end edge that may never arrive
findings.detail: subagent/start stores the live Agent object in a Map keyed by runId, and only subagent/end removes it. If the end edge is not emitted for a given runId, whether a child torn down through a path that skips the paired event, a start that races the bridge own disposal window, or a runId collision across a reload, the Map holds a strong reference to the Agent and transitively its entire session event log for the process lifetime. That leak scales with the number of subagents started. The comment on lines 121-125 states the requirement explicitly, saying every retained entry relies on that paired end and a producer that can omit it must provide another release edge, but no such edge exists: there is no agent/disposed fallback and no cap on the map. The SubagentStop hook is also skipped entirely in that case, so the audit trail is silently incomplete.

findings.title: The /permission command and the public set API write the approval-policy knob through different writers with different model-visible effects
findings.detail: apply takes the approval writer as a callback so the two entry points can diverge, and they do. The /permission command passes a closure around ctx.approval.setPolicy, which appends the durable approval/policy event and injects a user message telling the model the policy changed. The public set method passes a closure around setApprovalPolicy, which appends the same durable event but injects nothing. A deployment that switches presets through set therefore leaves the model runtime-context snapshot and its switch notice stale relative to the actual permission state, while a user switching through the command sees the notice. apply is also the only place the sandbox knob is written, so the asymmetry is easy to miss and hard to notice in testing.

clusters.summary:
Overall the cluster is unusually well-hardened: the LLM seam, DeepSeek adapter, pi-ai adapter, LSP framing/translation, gateway reflection boundary, and the client Host trust fence all show deliberate threat modelling (closed-union switches, structural guards on every wire payload, credential snapshots bound to endpoints, exact rpcId echo discipline, JSON-safety asserts on every typert argument and result). I found no exploitable secret leak, no sandbox escape, and no data-loss path.

The gaps that survived verification cluster around one theme: defensive code that is *structurally* thorough but *numerically* or *terminologically* under-constrained at the boundary with an untrusted peer. The highest-impact one is MCP `tools/list` pagination, where trusting an external server's cursor unbounds a loop that plugin activation and host unload both await — a third-party process can wedge the harness indefinitely. The LSP connection drops string-id JSON-RPC responses (JSON-RPC-legal) and, because the resulting hang is an abort rather than a transport failure, the poisoned instance is never evicted from the workspace pool. Two adapter issues are cost bugs rather than correctness bugs: pi-ai's first offload pass budgets against master attachment bytes instead of request bytes, over-trimming images by roughly 4x, and DeepSeek's stale-file recovery fires on any status whose body merely mentions a file, duplicating an upload and a POST for a failure that was never retriable.

On the trust boundary, the SDK JSON-RPC server is the weakest link: it casts wire params with `as unknown as` and commits caller-supplied `contentBlocks` straight into the durable session log, so a caller can inject a forged `tool-result` block — the exact prompt-injection surface the brief targets — while the sibling ACP bridge validates the same shape properly. The stdio transport it sits on writes frames fire-and-forget with no 'error' listener, so a broken parent pipe becomes an uncaught EPIPE crash rather than a clean exit. Finally, `isLoopbackHostname` accepts non-canonical IPv6 and zero-padded IPv4 spellings of 127.0.0.1, which is the sole Host fence for the loopback-pinned privileged method set on plain HTTP; the adjacent `assertTrustedAuthority` already refuses exactly this class of spelling elsewhere in the same package.

The remaining findings (http-bridge's uncontained handler rejection, the bare-text 500 on shared RPC channels, the empty synthesized tool-call id, and the collapsed per-image MCP diagnostic) are narrower but share the same shape: a failure path that reaches the wrong layer or loses the one piece of information the next consumer needed. None of them block shipping; the MCP pagination bound, the LSP string-id case, and the SDK content validation are the three worth fixing first.

findings.title: tools/list pagination loop is unbounded — a buggy MCP server can hang plugin activation and unload forever
findings.detail:
`syncTools` drains pages with a bare `do { ... cursor = response.nextCursor } while (cursor)`. There is no page cap, no seen-cursor set, and no total-tools cap, and the cursor is trusted verbatim from an external third-party process reached over stdio or HTTP.

Consequences when a server returns a non-empty `nextCursor` that never repeats a terminal page:
1. `connectGeneration` awaits `enqueueSync`, and `apply()` awaits `connection.ready` (`connection.ts:177`) — the plugin's activation never settles, so `failOnStartupError` never fires and the whole Cordis fiber never activates.
2. `enqueueSync` chains onto `syncChain`, so the never-settling sync permanently wedges the supervisor's serialized sync queue.
3. `dispose()` awaits `syncChain` (`connection.ts:346`), so HMR unload / host shutdown also hangs forever — teardown is blocked behind an untrusted peer.

The reconnect supervisor cannot help: the attempt never fails, it just never completes, so `maxAttempts` is never consulted. A page cap (or cursor-history check) would contain this at the trust boundary.

findings.title: Responses carrying a string JSON-RPC id are silently dropped, permanently poisoning the pooled LSP instance
findings.detail:
`dispatch()` accepts a server->client *request* for a string id (line 246), but a *response* is gated on `typeof id === 'number'`. JSON-RPC 2.0 allows string request ids and requires the server to echo the id exactly as received; a conforming-but-non-numeric-id server therefore gets every response discarded.

`pending` is never cleared and never rejects, so `LspConnection.request()` hangs. In `LspInstance.runQuery` that surfaces as the caller's abort/tool timeout — and because the rejection is the abort error rather than the connection's retained `closeReason`, `isTransportFailure(error)` is false, so `startTeardown()` never runs and neither does the `finally` eviction at `instance.ts:296` (`instance.dead` stays false: not closed, not disposed, not failed). The dead instance stays in `LocalLspProvider.instances` and every subsequent query for that workspace reuses it and hangs again until restart.

`dispatch` already treats `typeof id === 'string' || typeof id === 'number'` as sufficient for the request branch (correctly — that is how a numeric-id client request is distinguished), so the response branch dropping the string case is an inconsistency inside one function, not a protocol decision. No test in `connection.spec.ts`/`instance.spec.ts` exercises a string response id.

findings.title: Turns cancelled by a hook/owner settle as `end_turn`; ACP has no out-of-band `cancelled` and only `interrupted` maps to it
findings.detail:
`settleAfterQuiescence` resolves `end.kind === 'aborted' ? 'end_turn' : ...` (line 206) and `turnEndToStopReason` maps `'interrupted' -> 'cancelled'`, `'aborted' -> 'end_turn'`. The only path that yields ACP `cancelled` is `inflight.cancelRequested` or `endReason === undefined`.

ACP defines `cancelled` as "the agent cancelled the prompt (via session/cancel) or the agent-side session was aborted". A turn aborted by a hook or another owner is precisely agent-side cancellation, so the bridge misreports it as `end_turn`.

Unlike other channels, ACP gives the automation client no other signal: `session/update` emits only committed `agent_message_chunk`, and no `stop_reason` update is sent. So a client that prompts and waits on the response cannot distinguish "the model finished" from "the model was aborted mid-turn and produced nothing" — the observable contract is identical, and there is no partial-output marker either (the aborted stream's blocks go to `interruptedBlocks()` in the agent loop, not to ACP). This makes cancellation effectively invisible to ACP consumers.

findings.title: JSON-RPC output writes are fire-and-forget with no callback and no 'error' listener — a broken stdio pipe becomes an uncaught EPIPE crash
findings.detail:
`write()` calls `this.output.write(json)\n` with neither a completion callback nor any error containment, while the adjacent `flush()` (line 166-173) *does* take a callback and reject on error — so the module already knows the stream can fail, it just does not handle it on the real data path.

In production the output is `process.stdout` (`sdk/server/src/index.ts:55`). When that is a pipe (SDK-managed transports, `HarnessClient` spawns the runtime with `stdio: ['pipe','pipe','pipe']`), a reader that goes away produces EPIPE; Node emits `'error'` on the stream, and with no listener the process dies with an uncaught exception rather than a clean exit. `start()` only attaches `input.on('error')` — the output stream is never guarded.

This is not only a shutdown race. `HarnessSdkJsonRpcServer`'s constructor registers `ctx.on('session/event', ...)` / `agent/status` / `session/created` / `subagent/end`, all of which call `this.transport.notify(...)` synchronously. Any of those firing while the parent's read end is gone (parent crashed, pipe torn down mid-teardown) writes to a broken stdout. No `process.stdout.on('error', ...)` is installed anywhere in the repo.

findings.title: First-pass image offload budgets against master attachment bytes, so the second pass drops roughly 4x more images than the bound needs
findings.detail:
`toPiContextWithImages` runs `offloadRequestImagesWithPolicy` twice. The first pass (line 229-234) supplies `byteLength: ref => Math.min(ref.bytes, requestImagePolicy.maxBytes)`, and `offloadRequestImagesWithPolicy` is called with `representation: 'base64'` (line 230) — so `collectImageLengths` applies `base64Length(bytes) = ceil(bytes/3)*4` to the *master* attachment size (`llm/llm/src/content.ts:72-75`).

`ref.bytes` is the durable master attachment; the request version the provider actually sees has already been pixel/byte-capped by `readImageRequest`. So the first pass measures an over-estimate and over-removes: with the default 20 MiB bound and ~1 MiB request images, a conversation with 15 request images (≈20 MiB base64) but 2 MiB masters budgets 40 MiB and trims the oldest ones anyway. Only after the trimmed set is materialized does the exact second pass (line 236-241) run — on messages that have already had images irreversibly replaced with placeholders.

The DeepSeek adapter got this right: it passes `representation: 'raw'` for the estimate and a `byteLength` against the exact request version (`llm-deepseek/src/adapter.ts:537-544`). pi-ai inlines every image into every request body, so the over-trim shows up as lost conversation images for long image-heavy sessions.

findings.title: Stale-file retry fires on any HTTP status whose body merely mentions a file id — a non-retriable INVALID_REQUEST becomes a duplicate upload plus an immediate re-send
findings.detail:
`staleFile` is computed as `usedFiles.length > 0 && providerRejectedFileId(detail)` with no status gate. `providerRejectedFileId` only pattern-matches the joined `code`/`type`/`message` text (`/\bfile.../` + `/expired|not found|deleted|.../`) — so a 429 or 500 whose message happens to contain "file" and "not found" (a proxy/gateway error mentioning files, a rate-limit detail quoting the request path, etc.) is classified as a stale file id.

The recovery then (a) invalidates the *correct* cached mapping and (b) `continue`s the request loop with `body` unchanged. Nothing between the offload at line 537 and `JSON.stringify(body)` at line 601 re-runs when `representation` is still `'file'`, and the cached id has just been deleted from the local index — so `ensureUploaded` re-uploads the identical image. The POST is then re-issued with the same payload. If it fails again, `fileAttempt === 1` drops out of the branch and throws.

Net effect on one misclassified transient error: one wasted full image upload plus one duplicated POST — a double cost for a failure that was never retryable. `providerRejectedNormalizedImage` (line 646) correctly gates on `response.status === 400`; the stale-file path should carry an equivalent status gate.

findings.title: SDK `session/prompt` commits caller-supplied `contentBlocks` verbatim as a durable user message with no content validation
findings.detail:
`handleRequest` dispatches `params as unknown as SessionPromptParams` and `prompt()` then does `createUserMessage({ content: params.contentBlocks, source: { kind: 'user' } })`. `createUserMessage`/`createMessage` (`llm/src/message.ts:192-200`) only brand an id and deep-freeze — they do not validate the block vocabulary, roles, or nesting. The blocks go straight into the durable session log and later into every model request.

A `contentBlocks` payload containing a `{ type: 'tool-result', toolCallId: <any id>, content: [...], isError: false }` block is therefore admitted as a *user* message and reaches the model as an authoritative tool result for a call the model never made — the prompt-injection surface this cluster hunts for. `initialize`'s fields are equally unchecked (`this.model = params.model`, `this.cwd = resolve(params.cwd)` — a non-string cwd reaches `path.resolve` and throws a raw TypeError instead of a JSON-RPC invalid-params).

This is a real asymmetry: the ACP bridge validates the same boundary (`acp/src/content.ts:132-148` rejects unsupported block types before building the message) and the SDK protocol types claim `{ sessionId: string; contentBlocks: ContentBlock[] }`, but nothing on the wire enforces it. Some validation mirroring `admitAcpPrompt`'s closed-union switch belongs here.

findings.title: Loopback classifier accepts non-canonical IPv6 spellings and IPv4-mapped IPv6, widening the Host fence in a loopback-only deployment
findings.detail:
`isLoopbackHostname` special-cases exactly the strings `'localhost'` and `'[::1]'`. WHATWG URL also emits bracketed `'[::ffff:127.0.0.1]'` for a request to `http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]/...`, and the IPv4 branch only checks `parts.length === 4 && parts[0] === '127'` with a regex of 1-3 digits per octet — so `'127.000.000.001'`, `'127.0.0.001'`, `'127.0.00.1'` and `'127.00.0.1'` all return true. All of those are legal, distinct `Host` header spellings; every one of them passes the fence.

This matters most where `isTrustedApiRequest` is called with an empty trust list, which is the loopback pinning of the whole privileged plane (`PRIVILEGED_METHODS` in `client/connection/src/index.ts:145-148`, and the `'loopback'` authority in `rpc-host.ts:82`). For a rebound page served over plain HTTP there is no Origin and no Fetch-Metadata on navigations and image reads, so the Host check is the entire defence and it is what a rebinding attacker writes. The IPv6-mapped case is the sharper one: on an IPv6-capable stack `::ffff:127.0.0.1` is a routable form of loopback that a resolver can name.

Compare `assertTrustedAuthority` (`api-request-trust.ts:54-58`), which deliberately refuses anything WHATWG would rewrite precisely because a non-canonical spelling must "fail the load loudly instead of being ignored until requests 403 or quietly changing the grant". The loopback predicate has no such normalization.

findings.title: bridge() does not contain a rejection from apiHandler.fetch — the shared /api carrier surfaces carrier faults as HTTP 400
findings.detail:
`bridge` awaits `apiHandler.fetch(request)` with no try/catch, so a rejection escapes to the webserver's per-request catch, which logs and answers `res.writeHead(400)` when headers are not yet sent (and `res.destroy()` when they are). `apiHandler` is the shared fetch handler composed by `createSharedFetchHandler`, whose non-intercepted path is the whole apiProxy (`rpc-host.ts:79` -> `toFetchHandler(apiProxy)`). Any carrier-level throw — a session that no longer resolves, a bad payload shape the two-level parse rejects by throwing, an abort — is therefore reported to the browser as **400 Bad Request**, i.e. the client's own fault, instead of a 500 or a protocol error envelope.

The downstream symptom is already visible on the browser side: `createWebConnectionRpc.call` throws `transport failure for ${channel}/${endpoint}: HTTP 400` (`client/rpc.ts:44-46`), losing the rpcId-correlated envelope entirely. Mid-stream (SSE downlinks share this bridge) the webserver instead destroys the socket with no error frame.

The bridge already owns an `AbortController` and is the module that documents "carrier vs business" separation; a try/catch around the fetch that emits a 500/envelope before the SSE body starts would keep host faults off the client's tab.
findings.evidence:
const response = await apiHandler.fetch(request)
  res.writeHead(response.status, Object.fromEntries(response.headers.entries()))

findings.title: closeBlock synthesizes `CallId('')` instead of a per-block identity when a tool call arrives with no id
findings.detail:
A tool-call block opened because the wire carried `tool_calls` deltas but never a `call.id` assembles to `{ id: CallId(''), name: block.name ?? '', ... }`. `CallId('')` is an empty string that survives `createMessage`/`deepFreeze` into the durable log and into the agent loop, where tool results are correlated by call id — two such blocks collide, and every subsequent tool-result message for the second call lands on the first.

`BlockAssembler.assemble` handles exactly this case by synthesizing a stable per-index id (`llm/src/assembler.ts:126`: `id: partial.toolCallId ?? CallId(`call-${index}`)`), and the same file's sibling `name: block.name ?? ''` silently permits an unnamed tool call with no diagnostic. The OpenAI-compatible wire does send `call.id` on the first delta, so this needs a non-conforming gateway/proxy — but the module is explicitly written at a network trust boundary ("Defensive: fields that the MCP spec declares required ... are guarded with fallbacks because this is a network trust boundary" appears across this cluster), and the analogous empty-credential case in the same package is hard-failed via `assertUsableApiKey` rather than passed through.

findings.title: Handler throw on a shared RPC channel answers a bare-text HTTP 500 instead of a server-response envelope
findings.detail:
`rpcFetchHandler` catches a rejection from `handler(...)` and returns `new Response(`handler failure: ${String(error)}`, { status: 500 })` — plain text, not `{ type: 'server-response', rpcId, result }`.

Two concrete consequences: (1) `client/rpc.ts` only builds the `RpcResult` from a parseable envelope, so the caller sees `transport failure for ...: HTTP 500` and loses the rpcId correlation the protocol exists to provide; (2) `String(error)` renders a non-Error throw as `[object Object]`, discarding the message. The typert gateway itself is well-behaved (`rpcFailure` in `api/gateway/src/index.ts:639-657` converts every throw into `{ ok: false, error }`), so this only bites handlers registered by other plugins on `ctx.connection.rpc.handle` — but that is a public registration seam with no contract enforcement, and the module already has `errorResponse(rpcId, error)` two functions below that could carry a synthetic rpcId.

`rpcFetchHandler` also has no request-signal propagation guard: the `request.signal` passed to `handler` is the bridge's abort controller, which is fine, but the 500 path does not distinguish an abort from a real failure.

findings.title: One unadmittable image in an MCP result collapses every image block to the same generic diagnostic
findings.detail:
`prepareImageProjection`'s final `catch` (the `attachments.saveImages(decoded)` path) projects *every* image block through `block => ({ type: 'text', text: imageDiagnostic(block, reason) })`, dropping the `index` argument. When the batch fails, every image in the result therefore gets the identical reason string, so the model has no way to tell which of N images was rejected by admission.

The function already threads `index` correctly in the two earlier branches (`validationErrors.get(index)`, and `byIndex.get(index)`), and `imageDiagnostic(block, reason)` renders `block.mimeType` — so with one bad image among several, all N lines read the same mime type and the same reason, actively misinforming about which bytes were refused. Passing `(block, index)` and reporting the per-index reason where `saveImages` provides one (or explicitly naming that the batch is all-or-nothing) would keep the diagnostic honest.

clusters.summary: Reviewed ~39k lines across src/math, src/trainer, src/multimodal, src/agi, tools and bench. The cluster is in better shape than the file sizes suggest — the earlier "bug census" passes fixed a lot (softmax max-subtraction, subnormal FP8 encoding, lock-order inversions, empty-input pointer underflow), and src/agi is unusually honest about being non-functional rather than pretending. The real damage is concentrated in the distributed-training and SIMD layers. The single worst defect is that DDP never synchronizes gradients at all: build_buckets() fills Bucket::size but leaves Bucket::numel at 0, and allreduce_bucket() sizes every collective off numel, so ctx_.all_reduce is called with a count of 0 and every rank silently trains on its own local gradients. The ASYNC mode is independently broken twice over (a lock_guard whose scope ends before the work, and a self-deadlock on a non-recursive mutex). On the numerics side, the default AVX2 GELU kernel uses a 9th-order Taylor erf series that diverges past |x|~2 and is reachable from the transformer and MoE forward paths, and the primary AdamW optimizer applies bias correction twice, so every step is scaled by sqrt(1-beta2^t) — about 1% of the correct magnitude at t=1 under LLM-typical beta2. Memory-safety issues are narrower but real: an 8-wide AVX2 RoPE kernel that strides by 4, double-rotating most lanes and writing 16 bytes past the buffer; a ViT forward that collapses the batch dim and then over-reads; and a single shared fallback flag that turns a VirtualAlloc pointer into a free() call. Build-wide AVX2 plus a force-defined __AVX2__ macro on MSVC quietly voids every runtime CPU-dispatch check in the tree. tools/ and bench/ came out clean — the earlier hardening on those held up.

findings.title: DDP all-reduce is a silent no-op: Bucket::numel is never initialized
findings.detail: build_buckets() (lines 60-83) only ever writes current.size; Bucket::numel (include/quant/ddp.h:21) stays at its default 0 forever — there is no assignment to it anywhere in the tree. allreduce_bucket() exclusively reads bucket.numel, so the standard path calls ctx_.all_reduce(buf, 0), which adds/copies 0 elements. Every rank therefore keeps only its own local gradient and the ranks never converge. Worse, the TOP_K_SPARSE branch is gated on `bucket.numel > 0` so it never runs, and the FP8 branch (no numel gate) allocates an empty vector, does nothing, then skips the data all-reduce entirely — it just divides the local, unsynchronized gradient by world_size, corrupting the gradient scale on top of the missing reduction. DDP silently degrades to N independent single-rank trainings that drift apart.

findings.title: ASYNC DDP lock_guard scope ends before the work it was meant to protect
findings.detail: The lock_guard is declared inside the if-body, so it is destroyed at line 106 — before the allreduce loop on lines 108-110 begins. ASYNC DDP therefore acquires no mutual exclusion at all: a caller thread running sync_gradients() walks and rewrites the shared bucket.buffer tensors concurrently with async_sync_loop() doing the same, producing torn/corrupted gradient buckets. The fix is to hoist the guard out of the if so its lifetime spans the loop (or return early when not ASYNC).

findings.title: ASYNC DDP self-deadlocks: async_sync_loop locks async_mutex_ then calls sync_gradients which locks it again
findings.detail: async_sync_loop() takes async_mutex_ (line 353) and then calls sync_gradients() (line 354). sync_gradients() re-acquires the same mutex at line 105 in ASYNC mode. async_mutex_ is a plain std::mutex (include/quant/ddp.h:89), not a recursive_mutex, so this is a self-deadlock (and formally UB). The very first iteration of the background thread hangs forever, and because ~DistributedDataParallel() joins that thread, DDPMode::ASYNC cannot be destructed either.

findings.title: AdamW applies the v bias-correction twice, scaling every update by sqrt(1-beta2^t)
findings.detail: Line 99 folds sqrt(bias_corr2)/bias_corr1 into lr_adj, but line 115's denominator also divides v by bias_corr2. Expanding: implemented = lr * sqrt(bc2)/bc1 * m / (sqrt(v/bc2) + eps), while correct AdamW is lr/bc1 * m / (sqrt(v/bc2) + eps). The ratio is sqrt(bc2) < 1, so every step under-updates. With the common LLM settings beta2=0.9999 this is ~1% of the correct step at t=1 and still ~20% low at t=1000. Adam::step (lines 183-185) in the same file does it correctly, which is strong evidence the AdamW form is a transcription bug rather than a deliberate choice. This is the optimizer instantiated by trainer_core.cpp:1261, finetune.cpp:18 and moe_trainer.cpp, i.e. the default training path.
findings.evidence:
float lr_adj = lr * std::sqrt(bias_corr2) / bias_corr1;   // line 99
...
            p[i] -= lr_adj * m[i] / (std::sqrt(v[i] / bias_corr2) + eps_);  // line 115

findings.title: AVX2 gelu uses a 9th-order Taylor erf series that diverges past |x|~2
findings.detail: gelu is computed as 0.5*x*(1+erf(x/sqrt(2))) where 'erf' is the truncated Taylor series x - x^3/3 + x^5/10 - x^7/42 + x^9/216 with no range reduction. That series is only accurate for |x| << 1: at x=1.5 it is ~6% off, at x=2 it returns 2.09 instead of erf(2)=0.9953, and by x=2.5 it returns 11.49 instead of 0.9996. Since the input is scaled by 1/sqrt(2), gelu(v) is already badly wrong for |v| > ~2.8 and unbounded garbage beyond that — while the scalar tail (line 299) uses the exact std::erf. There is no range check or fallback, and the AVX2 kernel is the default: this function is the GELU used by transformer.cpp:578, moe_core.cpp:85, moe_model.cpp:636 and backend.cpp:123/1668. Any model configured with GELU FFN gets catastrophically wrong activations for typical post-LayerNorm magnitudes. The identical divergent series is duplicated in math_avx2_vec.cpp:285-298 (vec_gelu).

findings.title: AVX2 is enabled project-wide (and __AVX2__ force-defined on MSVC), defeating every runtime CPU-dispatch check
findings.detail: add_compile_options(/arch:AVX2) and add_definitions(-D__AVX2__) are global, so every translation unit in the project — tools, bench, server, all of src — is compiled with AVX2 as the baseline. On GCC/Clang the same applies via global -mavx2 -mfma (lines 45-47). Two consequences: (1) the compiler may emit VEX-encoded instructions anywhere, so detect_cpu_features() guards in simd_math.cpp / kernel are dead weight and the binary SIGILLs on any pre-Haswell CPU (Sandy/Ivy Bridge, all Atom); (2) on MSVC the forced -D__AVX2__ makes every `#ifdef __AVX2__` header guard — including include/quant/detail/exp_avx2.h and include/quant/simd_math.h — unconditionally active regardless of the flag. The whole runtime-dispatch architecture in this codebase is illusory. AVX2 flags must be applied per-target on the kernels that actually dispatch at runtime (quant_kernel, quant_math), not globally.
findings.evidence:
if(QUANT_AVX2)
    add_compile_options(/arch:AVX2)
    add_definitions(-D__AVX2__)
  endif()

findings.title: rope_avx2 strides 8-wide loads/stores by 4, double-rotating most lanes and writing 16 bytes past the row
findings.detail: The loop condition is `i + 4 <= half_dim; i += 4` but every _mm256_loadu/_mm256_storeu touches 8 floats. Two independent defects: (1) iteration i writes pairs [i, i+7] and iteration i+4 writes [i+4, i+11], so every pair from index 4 upward is rotated twice instead of once — the returned Q/K is wrong for nearly the whole head; (2) the second store targets `q + pos*head_dim + i + half_dim` with 8 floats, and with i up to half_dim-4 that reaches index head_dim+3 inside the row, i.e. 4 floats past the end of the row. For the last position this is a 16-byte heap write past the end of the q/k buffer, and the corresponding cos_cache/sin_cache loads overrun the cache as well. The correct stride is 8 (the comment '4 complex pairs = 8 floats' is itself confused — 8 floats of q0123 are 8 real parts, i.e. 8 pairs). The shipped unit test uses head_dim=2, for which `i+4 <= 1` never holds, so it exercises only the scalar tail and cannot catch this. The function is exported from the public header quant/simd_math.h.

findings.title: gemv_avx2 horizontal reduction drops the upper 128-bit lane, returning ~half the dot product
findings.detail: The reduction is hadd(hadd(lo128, hi128), lo128) then cvtss. hadd(lo,hi) yields [lo0+lo1, lo2+lo3, hi0+hi1, hi2+hi3]; the outer hadd's element 0 is therefore (lo0+lo1)+(lo2+lo3) — only accumulators 0..3. Accumulators 4..7 (the upper half of the K loop) are discarded, so y = alpha * (first-half dot product) + beta*y. The correct pattern, used everywhere else in this file and in math_avx2.cpp:156-162, is to first _mm_add_ps(hi, lo) element-wise and then hadd twice. No in-tree caller currently reaches simd::gemv (only tests/), but it is a public symbol of the installed math library and silently returns wrong answers on any AVX2 machine.
findings.evidence:
float s = _mm_cvtss_f32(_mm_hadd_ps(
            _mm_hadd_ps(_mm256_castps256_ps128(sum),
                        _mm256_extractf128_ps(sum, 1)),
            _mm256_castps256_ps128(sum)));

findings.title: VisionTransformer::forward drops every batch but the last, then OOB-reads when extracting CLS tokens
findings.detail: normed_x is allocated as {S, D} — a single batch slice — outside the batch loop, and line 223-224 copies each batch's result into it, so batches 0..B-2 are overwritten and only the last survives. Then `x = normed_x` replaces the {B,S,D} tensor with {S,D}, so at line 233 `x.dim(1)` is now D rather than S and the CLS extraction reads `xd + b * D * D` from a buffer that only holds S*D floats. For a typical ViT (D=768, S=197, B=2) b=1 starts at offset 589,824 floats into a 151,296-float buffer — a multi-megabyte heap over-read. The allocation should be {B, S, D} and written per-batch, and the stride at line 233 must use S, not x.dim(1).

findings.title: Single cpu_malloc_fallback_ flag makes the next free() of a VirtualAlloc'd region call free() on it
findings.detail: allocate_cpu() may fall back to std::malloc when VirtualAlloc fails (line 386) and sets the single boolean cpu_malloc_fallback_ = true. deallocate_cpu() then frees whichever pointer it is handed using that flag and immediately resets it. So one failed VirtualAlloc poisons the flag for the entire engine: the very next deallocate_cpu() of a *successfully VirtualAlloc'd* region takes the `cpu_malloc_fallback_` branch and calls std::free() on VirtualAlloc memory — heap corruption. The flag must be tracked per allocation (e.g. a side map from ptr -> allocator), not as one shared bit.

findings.title: ZeROOffloadManager::shard_gradient silently drops the tail remainder, and reset_stats() rewinds the state allocator
findings.detail: shard_size = total / world_size truncates, so start = rank*shard_size and end = min(start+shard_size, total) never covers [shard_size*world_size, total). Every gradient element past the last full shard is excluded from every rank's shard and therefore never reduced — the optimizer applies a wrong (stale/zero) update to those parameters, silently, and only when numel is not a multiple of world_size. Separately, line 162 reset_stats() zeroes cpu_buffer_used_, which is the bump-allocator cursor holding live Adam m/v state rather than a statistic; the next offload_optimizer_state() then reuses the start of the buffer and overwrites previously saved optimizer state. Finally the whole class appears to be dead API — AdamWOptimizer in the same file never calls offload/reload, and its `zero_(ZeROConfig{cfg_.learning_rate > 0})` ties ZeRO enablement to the learning rate being positive, which it always is, so offload is attempted while nothing wires it up.

findings.title: linear_forward_fp8 re-transposes and re-quantizes the entire weight matrix on every forward
findings.detail: The FP8 slow path (used whenever use_fp8 && !AutogradEngine::enabled(), i.e. the default inference configuration for an FP8 model — Attention::forward line 302 routes q/k/v/o through it) allocates a fresh std::vector<float> of in_dim*out_dim and transpose-copies the whole weight, then math::fp8_gemm re-quantizes A and B to FP8 and immediately de-quantizes them back to FP32 before a scalar triple loop. For a 7B model that is an O(numel) FP32 transpose plus an O(numel) FP8 round-trip per layer per token, and the inner GEMM is not vectorized at all. The comment at line 509 acknowledges the transpose but not the repeated quantization; the weight should be quantized once at load time and cached. Same shape of waste exists in math.cpp:663 fp8_gemm's scalar fallback.
